content_html:
Diffusion of Innovations

Diffusion of Innovations (Everett M. Rogers) explains how new ideas, products, and practices spread through social systems over time via communication channels and social influence. Adoption follows characteristic processes and population patterns.

Innovation‑Decision Process

Knowledge — exposure to the innovation.
Persuasion — forming a favorable or unfavorable attitude.
Decision — adopt or reject.
Implementation — put to use; adapt to context.
Confirmation — seek reinforcement; continue or discontinue.

Feedback is present at each stage (trial results, peer signals).

Adopter Categories (typical shares)

Innovators (~2.5%) — venturesome; resource access.
Early Adopters (~13.5%) — opinion leaders; reduce uncertainty.
Early Majority (~34%) — deliberate; many informal social links.
Late Majority (~34%) — skeptical; adopt under pressure/norms.
Laggards (~16%) — tradition‑bound; limited resources.

Shares are descriptive, not prescriptive; vary by context.

S‑Curve (Cumulative Adoption) and Bell Curve (Adopter Distribution)

The bell curve shows the rate of adoption at each time slice; the S‑curve shows cumulative adoption.

Determinants of Adoption

Relative advantage — perceived benefit over current practice.
Compatibility — fit with values, needs, infrastructure.
Complexity — ease of understanding/using.
Trialability — can it be tried incrementally?
Observability — visibility of results to others.

Feedback Loops & the Membrane

Positive loops: social proof accelerates adoption (viral spread).
Negative loops: norms/regulation slow or stabilize.
Expansion ↔ Refinement: novelty enters via innovators; institutions codify and standardize.
